steps.title: Where to start: split each term into a difference
steps.body:
Every denominator is a product of two consecutive whole numbers, $n(n+1)$. That is the clue for a popular trick: such a fraction is the difference of two simpler fractions,
$$\frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1}$$

steps.title: Rewrite the sum and watch it cancel
steps.body:
Now the sum becomes
$$\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{5}\right) + \cdots$$
Each negative piece is cancelled by the positive piece right after it. So if you stop after $N$ terms, everything in the middle is gone and only $1 - \frac{1}{N+1}$ is left.

your_turn.prompt: What is the sum of just the first four terms?
your_turn.answer: $1 - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{5}$, because everything between the first $1$ and the last $-\frac{1}{5}$ cancels.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: The sum goes on forever, so we look at what $1 - \frac{1}{N+1}$ approaches as $N$ gets larger and larger. The piece $\frac{1}{N+1}$ shrinks toward $0$, so the sums get as close to $1$ as we like. Careful: no finite number of terms ever reaches $1$ exactly, but the value of the infinite sum is this limit. The answer is **$1$**.
